scenes.tts: Why does a ganglion cell answer a small spot better than light spread over the whole retina?
scenes.visual: Title card: Centre Minus Surround. A ganglion cell with a spike train: a small spot gives dense spikes, a full field fewer. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: Why does a ganglion cell answer a small spot better than light spread over the whole retina?

scenes.tts: In nineteen fifty-three, Stephen Kuffler recorded single ganglion cells in cats. He shone small spots of light onto the retina.
scenes.caption: In 1953, Stephen Kuffler recorded single ganglion cells in cats. He shone small spots of light onto the retina.
scenes.visual: A cat retina with an electrode near one ganglion cell; small spots of light projected onto it. Label: Kuffler, 1953.
scenes.narration: In 1953, Stephen Kuffler recorded single ganglion cells in cats. He shone small spots of light onto the retina.

scenes.tts: A spot in the middle of the field made one cell fire faster.
scenes.visual: A spot on the field's centre; the spike train below becomes dense while the spot is on.
scenes.narration: A spot in the middle of the field made one cell fire faster.

scenes.tts: A spot on a ring around the middle made the same cell fall silent. When the light went off, it fired.
scenes.visual: An annulus lights the ring; the spike train goes sparse, then a burst of spikes at light-off.
scenes.narration: A spot on a ring around the middle made the same cell fall silent. When the light went off, it fired.

scenes.tts: That is an on-centre cell. An off-centre cell does the mirror image.
scenes.caption: That is an ON-centre cell. An OFF-centre cell does the mirror image.
scenes.visual: The field drawn as a plus centre and minus ring. Beside it the mirror: minus centre, plus ring. Labels: ON-centre, OFF-centre.
scenes.narration: That is an ON-centre cell. An OFF-centre cell does the mirror image.

scenes.tts: The centre comes from the bipolar cells that contact the ganglion cell. The surround comes from cells that act sideways.
scenes.visual: Circuit view: bipolar cells under the centre wire to the ganglion cell's dendrites. Sideways cells spread out to the ring.
scenes.narration: The centre comes from the bipolar cells that contact the ganglion cell. The surround comes from cells that act sideways.

scenes.tts: Horizontal cells do this in the outer retina, and amacrine cells add more in the inner retina. Both push the response the opposite way from the centre.
scenes.visual: Horizontal cells feed back onto cone terminals; amacrine cells add inhibition in the inner retina. Arrows from the surround oppose the centre's arrow. Label: mechanism of feedback still debated.
scenes.narration: Horizontal cells do this in the outer retina, and amacrine cells add more in the inner retina. Both push the response the opposite way from the centre.

scenes.tts: Now light the whole field, centre and surround together. More spikes than the best spot, fewer, or no change from the background?
scenes.visual: The full field lit. The spike train is hidden. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: Now light the whole field, centre and surround together. More spikes than the best spot, fewer, or no change from the background?

scenes.tts: In this example, fewer: forty-five spikes a second instead of sixty. Its surround cancels only part of the centre.
scenes.visual: The spike train returns: between the centre-spot rate and the background. On screen: background 20 spikes/s; centre +40; surround −15; full field 45. A spot-size curve rises, peaks at a spot about the size of the centre, then falls, staying above background. Label: worked example, this example's weights.
scenes.narration: In this example, fewer: 45 spikes a second instead of 60. Its surround cancels only part of the centre.
scenes.caption: In this example, fewer: 45 spikes a second instead of 60. Its surround cancels only part of the centre.

scenes.tts: So the cell reports contrast, a spot brighter than its surroundings, more than overall light level.
scenes.visual: Text on screen: contrast more than brightness.
scenes.narration: So the cell reports contrast, a spot brighter than its surroundings, more than overall light level.

scenes.tts: Now line up a row of on-centre cells across an edge, where light meets dark.
scenes.caption: Now line up a row of ON-centre cells across an edge, where light meets dark.
scenes.visual: A light/dark edge with a row of ON-centre fields across it, each with a rate bar.
scenes.narration: Now line up a row of ON-centre cells across an edge, where light meets dark.

scenes.tts: The cell right on the edge is not the winner. In this model, cells just on the bright side fire most. Their surrounds reach into the dark and subtract less.
scenes.visual: Bars show the change in firing from the dark-side baseline, from a symmetric linear difference-of-Gaussians model. The cell centred on the edge gets about half the uniform-light change; the tallest bars sit just on the bright side, above cells deep in the bright area. Their surround rings overlap the dark half.
scenes.narration: The cell right on the edge is not the winner. In this model, cells just on the bright side fire most. Their surrounds reach into the dark and subtract less.

scenes.tts: Cells just on the dark side fire least. The edge stands out across the population.
scenes.visual: The shortest bars, dipping below baseline, sit just on the dark side. The overshoot and undershoot frame the edge.
scenes.narration: Cells just on the dark side fire least. The edge stands out across the population.

scenes.tts: The same logic gives colour. One cone cannot tell a change in wavelength from a change in intensity.
scenes.visual: One cone's broad sensitivity curve. A dim light near its peak and a brighter light on its tail, with matched timing and the same effective catch, give matching mean graded responses under the same adaptation. Label: one cone cannot separate wavelength from intensity.
scenes.narration: The same logic gives colour. One cone cannot tell a change in wavelength from a change in intensity.

scenes.tts: Compare two cones with overlapping curves, and their ratio changes with wavelength. Turn the light up, and the ratio holds.
scenes.visual: M and L curves overlap, peaks near 530 and 560 nm. A readout shows the M to L ratio changing as the marker slides; an intensity slider moves both catches but not the ratio.
scenes.narration: Compare two cones with overlapping curves, and their ratio changes with wavelength. Turn the light up, and the ratio holds.

scenes.tts: But in pigment models the ratio can repeat. Set two wavelengths to the same L catch, and their M catches match too. The S cone catches far more of the shorter one, so it tells them apart.
scenes.visual: Label: pigment-template model. The marker finds two wavelengths, near 427 and 529 nm, with the same M to L reading. Their intensities are scaled to give equal L catch, and the M bars match too. The S curve appears: it catches far more at the shorter one. Label: what the S cone adds.
scenes.narration: But in pigment models the ratio can repeat. Set two wavelengths to the same L catch, and their M catches match too. The S cone catches far more of the shorter one, so it tells them apart.

scenes.tts: Here is the whole rule. One receptor cannot separate wavelength from intensity. The circuit compares.
scenes.visual: On screen: one receptor cannot separate wavelength from intensity; the circuit compares.
scenes.narration: Here is the whole rule. One receptor cannot separate wavelength from intensity. The circuit compares.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: ganglion cells send those comparisons to the brain as spikes.
scenes.visual: Spike trains leave along the optic nerve toward the brain.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: ganglion cells send those comparisons to the brain as spikes.
